p.title: The road to coordinates

events.label: Mohenjo-daro's streets laid out in a grid
events.info: Sindhu-Sarasvati cities had straight streets, mostly meeting at right angles (c. 2500 BCE).

events.label: Aryabhata describes positions of heavenly bodies
events.info: In the Aryabhatiya (499 CE) he gave angle-like coordinates for planets and stars.

events.label: Brahmagupta's rules for zero and negatives
events.info: Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE). Negatives let us name points left of and below the origin.

events.label: Al-Biruni locates cities by latitude and longitude
events.info: Around 1030 CE: two numbers fix a place on the Earth.

events.label: Omar Khayyam solves algebra with geometry
events.info: Around 1070 CE he solved cubic equations using geometric curves.

events.label: Descartes names every point with two numbers
events.info: La Géométrie (1637) joined algebra and geometry: the Cartesian plane.

p.challenge: Put these steps in the story of coordinates in time order, oldest first.
A room is 12 ft × 9 ft. Draw its floor map at 1 cm = 3 ft: drag the corner to make the map the right size.
p.winText: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cm and 9 ÷ 3 = 3 cm: a 4 cm × 3 cm map. (At 1 cm = 1 ft it would be 12 cm × 9 cm.)

p.challenge: Plot P(4, −3): 4 right, 3 down. Then Q(2, 5) and R(5, 2) (order matters!) and S(0, −2), which sits on the y-axis.
Plot a point B exactly 5 units from A(1, 2). Use distance = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]: try across 3 and up 4.
Plot A(2, 3), B(−2, 3), C(−2, −1) and D(2, −1). Same y gives a horizontal side, same x a vertical side. What shape is ABCD, and what is its perimeter?
A room is 12 ft × 10 ft with one corner at O(0, 0). Place a 4 ft × 2 ft table at the centre of the room: plot the table's four corners.
A(1, 1) and B(4, 1) share the same y. Drag C to (1, 5) so that AC is vertical: then ∠A = 90° and the sides are 3, 4 and 5.
Plot B between A(1, 1) and C(7, 9) so that A, B, C are collinear: AB + BC must equal AC = 10.
The circle x² + y² = 25 has centre O and radius 5. Plot a point exactly ON the circle (not inside, not outside).
Plot the two points of trisection P and Q of A(1, 2) and B(7, 11). Each step is one-third of the change: 6 ÷ 3 across and 9 ÷ 3 up.

p.winText: 3x − 12 = 0 gives x = 4: the line meets the x-axis at (4, 0). Check: p(4) = 12 − 12 = 0.

Draw F = (9/5)C + 32 (x = °C, y = °F): set the slope to 9/5 = 1.8 and the intercept to 32 (water freezes at 0 °C = 32 °F). Then read F at C = 5.
p.winText: Each 1 °C step is 1.8 °F. At C = 5, F = 9 + 32 = 41 °F.

p.winText: Both lines pass through (−1, 0), because a(−1) + a = 0 for every a.

p.title: Proof: √2 is irrational

nodes.info: Proof by contradiction: assume the opposite and look for trouble.

nodes.text: Square: p² = 2q², so p² is even

nodes.info: If p were odd, p² would be odd.

nodes.text: So q² is even, and q is even too
p and q both even contradicts 'lowest form': √2 is irrational

Shopkeepers find 49 × 51 = 50² − 1² = 2499. Try it small: choose a and b so (a + b)(a − b) = 7 × 3 = 21, then Rearrange to see a² − b².

p.winText: It cuts the x-axis at x = 1/3 and x = 3: a number and its reciprocal! 3 + 1/3 = 10/3.

p.title: Is it an identity?

nodes.info: The true identity is (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b².

p.challenge: Test the claim (a + b)² = a² + b² with a = 1 and b = 1. Press Next and choose the right branch.
Use 1 big x² tile, 7 x-strips and 12 unit squares. Find a and b so the tiles make the rectangle (x + a)(x + b) = x² + 7x + 12.
Splitting the middle term gives 2x² + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3). Build y = 2x² + 7x + 3 and check where it is zero.
p.winText: y = 0 at x = −1/2 (2x + 1 = 0) and x = −3 (x + 3 = 0): the factors show the zeros.

No chord is longer than a diameter (AB ≤ OA + OB = 2r). Drag the ends of the chord to make the longest chord possible.
A and B are 10 units apart. Plot the centre of the SMALLEST circle through A and B: it is on the perpendicular bisector of AB, as close to A as possible.
Triangle ABC has a right angle at A, with legs 6 and 8. Plot its circumcentre O, equally far from A, B and C. Where on the hypotenuse is it?
O is the centre; A and B lie on the circle, so OA = OB = r. Drag A or B to make OA = OB and see the base angles at A and B become equal.
Radius 5: chord AB = 8 and chord CD = 6 lie on opposite sides of O. Plot M and N, the feet of the perpendiculars from O (the midpoints of AB and CD). How far apart are the chords?
In a circle of radius 10, AB and CD are both 12-unit chords. Plot their midpoints M and N. Are equal chords the same distance from O?
O is the centre, M the foot of the perpendicular to the chord, OM = 8 cm. Drag A along the chord so that ∠M = 90° and OA = 17 cm (the radius). Then half-chord MA = √(17² − 8²).
Make arc AB subtend ∠AOB = 130° at the centre. What angle does it subtend at P on the major arc? Move P and check.
Make AB a diameter. Then move P anywhere on the circle: the angle in a semicircle is always 90°.
ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with ∠A = 75°. Opposite angles add to 180°. Make angle 1 = ∠A = 75° and read ∠C (angle 2).
p.winText: ∠C = 180° − 75° = 105°. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.

p.winText: 72° = 1/5 of a turn. A rim point of a 35 cm wheel travels 1/5 × 220 = 44 cm.

p.title: Chasing π

events.label: Archimedes traps π between 223/71 and 22/7
events.info: He used polygons with 96 sides (c. 250 BCE).

events.label: Liu Hui gets π ≈ 3.1416
events.info: In his commentary on the Nine Chapters (263 CE).

p.challenge: People approximated the mystery ratio π (circumference ÷ diameter) over centuries. Put these in time order.
Meena's circular rangoli has a border of 132 cm. Drag the radius to find r (C = 2πr, π = 22/7), then read its area.
22/7 = 3 1/7 ≈ 3.1429 is only an approximation: it is slightly MORE than π ≈ 3.1416. Drag the frog to 22/7.
Make a sector of radius 21 cm whose arc is 22 cm (arc = θ/360 × 2πr, π = 22/7). Its perimeter is then arc + 2r = 22 + 42.
A 1 × 9 rectangle has perimeter 20 but area only 9. Keep the perimeter 20 m and make the area as big as possible.
p.winText: 5 × 5: perimeter 20, area 25. Same perimeter does not mean same area!

p.challenge: Area of a parallelogram = base × perpendicular height (the slanted side does not count). Drag the corners to make an area of 24 sq cm.
This triangle has base 8 and height 6 (area 24). Slide only the top corner: the area stays the same between the same parallels. Then make a triangle with HALF the area, as a median does.
Base BC = 14 cm. Drag A until AB = 13 cm and AC = 15 cm. Heron: s = 21, area = √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6). Does the grid area agree?
ABCD is a square of side 10 (area 100). Plot the midpoints P, Q, R, S of its sides. Joining them makes a new square: what is its area?
Baudhayana squared a rectangle: keep the area of this 9 m × 4 m rectangle (36 m²) but turn it into a square.
A chord subtends 90° at the centre of a circle of radius 14 cm. Make that sector (area 154 sq cm). Minor segment = sector − triangle OAB = 154 − 98.
A circle fits inside a 14 cm square, touching all four sides. Drag the radius to make that circle (area 154 sq cm), then find the area outside it: 196 − 154.
The forecast says '70% chance of rain'. Spin the weather spinner: is rain impossible, less likely, equally likely, more likely or certain?
Roll a die once. The sample space is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Which outcomes are favourable for 'greater than 4'? Predict the probability, then roll.
On the 0–1 probability scale, drag the frog to P(a fair die shows 6). Is it nearer impossible (0) or certain (1)?

A factory found 3 faulty pens in 150. Predict P(faulty), then test 1000 pens. Expected faulty = P × 1000: how close is your count?
A die rolled 600 times showed 6 on 94 rolls (0.157). Predict the theoretical P(6), then roll 1000 times. Does the bar move closer?
Toss two coins. The sample space is {HH, HT, TH, TT}. What is P(exactly one head)? Predict, then toss.
A bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. Each ball is put back after it is drawn (with replacement), so the bag stays the same. What is P(red)?

So the sum of two odd numbers is always even ∎

x + 2y = 8 has solutions (0, 4), (2, 3) and (8, 0). Make the line y = mx + c pass through all three: every point on it is a solution.

Graph 2x + 3y = 12: plot the y-intercept (put x = 0), the x-intercept (put y = 0) and the check point with x = 3. Do all three lie on one line?
A line through A(1, 2) has slope 3. Plot the point B on it with x = 4: run 3, so the rise is 3 × 3.
Rewrite 4x − 2y + 6 = 0 as y = mx + d (m = −a/b, d = −c/b), then set the sliders to draw it.
Solve x + y = 10 and x − y = 2 graphically: draw y = −x + 10 and y = x − 2. Where do the lines meet?
p.winText: They meet at (6, 4): x = 6, y = 4. Check: 6 + 4 = 10 and 6 − 4 = 2.

p.challenge: Comparison method: y = 2x + 1 and y = 7 − x give 2x + 1 = 7 − x. Adding x to both sides gives 3x + 1 = 7. Solve it on the balance, then find y.
3x − 2y = 5 and 6x − 4y = 9: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = 1/2 but c₁/c₂ = 5/9. Both lines have slope 3/2. Set both slopes to 1.5: do the lines ever meet?
p.winText: Same slope, different intercepts: parallel lines, so the pair has NO solution.

p.challenge: Fraction x/y: clue 1 gives y = 2x + 2 and clue 2 gives y = 3x + 1. Comparing them: 2x + 2 = 3x + 1. Find the numerator x on the balance.
p.winText: x = 1 and y = 2 × 1 + 2 = 4, so the fraction is 1/4. Check: 2/4 = 1/2 and 1/3 ✓

p.challenge: Mahaviracharya's puzzle: adding and subtracting the two bills gave x + y = 13 and x − y = 3 (x = citron, y = wood-apple). Draw y = −x + 13 and y = x − 3 and read where they meet.
p.winText: They meet at (8, 5): a citron costs 8 and a wood-apple 5. Check: 9 × 8 + 7 × 5 = 107 ✓
